name: Maritime Oil Painting
description: Nineteenth-century marine oil painting for covers and hero scenes — loose visible brushwork, a pale ivory sky left open for a title, and sepia, ochre and gold weather over navy water.
style_bible: Nineteenth-century marine oil painting on primed canvas. Medium and surface: loose visible brushwork, oil laid in directional strokes that stay readable as paint, thin scumbled glazes in the sky and thicker impasto reserved for spray, cloud edges, and the lit crests of water, with fine craquelure and a warm varnish bloom over the whole surface. Edges and shapes: painterly and soft almost everywhere, sails and hulls held together by tone rather than outline, rigging suggested with a few dry-brushed hairlines rather than drawn thread by thread, horizon slightly broken and never ruler-straight. Palette: sepia, ochre, raw and burnt sienna, aged gold and warm ivory through the sky, moving to deep navy, slate green and cold grey in the water, with oxblood and a single muted vermilion reserved for the smallest accents — a pennant, a painted strake, a lantern. Lighting: soft diffused daylight from a low overcast sun, light entering from one side and passing through cloud rather than striking hard; luminous sky, no hard modern key light, no rim light, no artificial glow. Texture: canvas tooth visible through thin passages, dry-brush drag on rope and spar, granular sea spray, torn cloud with light behind it. Subject grammar: tall ships under wind-filled sail in weather, wooden hulls streaked with salt, masts, yards, standing rigging, boats pulling from a beach, period harbour towns with stone moles, warehouses and small craft — or, alternatively, a single anonymous period figure at three-quarter length in seafaring dress turned toward the viewer, weather in the coat and hair, face lit softly and never a recognisable individual. Framing: hold the sky pale, open and largely empty across the upper third to two-fifths of the canvas as deliberate negative space where a title can sit; place the vessel or figure low and to one side on a clear diagonal, keep the waterline below centre, and let atmosphere rather than detail carry the distance. Keep the contract content-independent: no fixed vessel, port, era detail, event, or copied composition.
